All aboard the Sliabh Luachra express…

Here’s yet another fine jig from Paudie O‘Connor & John O’Brien’s “Wind & Reeds” CD. This one I’ve actually known for some time, but I didn’t see it in the tune DB, and since I finally have a title for it (I hate posting tunes as “Gan Ainm”), here goes! The notes say that the tunes in this set (I’ll be posting the others next) were learned from Cork fiddler Connie O’Connell, who in turn got them from Denis Murphy. Enjoy!

Bill The Weaver’s, X:4

This setting appears in The Petrie Collection of Irish Music, part II, ed. Charles Villiers Stanford (1905), p. 207, no. 829 as “Cheer Up, Old Hag. Set by Lord Rosmore. From P. Coneely. 1845”.
The structure (which doesn’t appear in the score) is ABAB’A.

Re: Cheer Up Old Hag

I have been searching for info on a jig I learned from concertina teacher Tom McGonagle (County Down) as “Bill the Weaver”. It seems to be close to the Humours of Killarney and Cheer Up Old Hag, but with the two parts reversed. While trying to play the X4 version above in abc Navigator (I don’t read too well) I discovered that the time signature is wrong from that version. It’s actually a Slip Jig and should be 9/8 thus:
T: Cheer Up Old Hag
R: Slip jig
M: 9/8
L: 1/8
K: Gmaj

Bill The Weaver

I learned this jig from concertina player and teacher Tom McGonagle (County Down) in one of his 2020 online classes. It doesn’t match the Bill the Weaver listed on The Session as such (The Rolling Wave) but it is similar to some tunes listed here under ‘The Humours of Killarney’ and ‘Cheer up Old Hag’., but the parts are reversed. I like its simple structure nad it sounds like a sweet tune to me.
The tune has been recorded on a CD by Dylan Carlos, Cein Sweeney and John McCartin in a jig set with Jackson’s Rolling Jig and the Chapel Bell.

An Síoda Atá Id Vallait?

Title from CRE5.81. I think the note says Breathnach obtained it from an RTE recording from around 1940 of Pádraig O‘Keeffe. It also says it is a traditional air used as a slide. Apparently Owen Roe O’Sullivan (the great Munster poet from Sliabh Luachra, Knocknagree) used this air for one of his poems, Cois Abhan i nDé.
The song title might translate as Is that Silk in Your Wallet?
